rows.verified: The Control of Lead at Work Regulations require employers to prevent exposure to lead or, where prevention is not reasonably practicable, control it.
Employers should identify tasks that use lead or generate lead dust or fume and assess where significant exposure could occur.
Lead exposure should be reduced by limiting the number of people exposed, the amount of lead exposure and the duration of exposure.
Engineering, respiratory, administrative and behavioural controls must be used correctly and maintained in effective condition.
Employers should keep records that demonstrate lead-exposure controls are being sustained.
Employers should consult an HSE-appointed doctor about appropriate medical surveillance for lead work.
Suitable washing and separate storage arrangements are needed to prevent contamination of clean clothing and personal areas.
Lead exposure can affect blood, the nervous system, kidneys and reproductive health.
Lead controls depend on lead form, process, dust or fume generation, airborne and biological monitoring, worker age or health, hygiene and control performance.
Lead evidence is substance-, task-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level illness probability.
Employers should identify workplace sources of ionising radiation, assess significant risks and control exposure.
Depending on risk level, work with ionising radiation may require notification, registration or consent through HSE.
Exposure to ionising radiation must be kept as low as reasonably practicable and must not exceed specified dose limits.
Exposure restriction should first use engineering controls and design features, then safe systems of work, with personal protective equipment as a last resort.
Competent radiation-protection advice is required for work with ionising radiation where the regulations apply.
HSE guidance covers approved dosimetry, dose monitoring, assessment and recording for relevant ionising-radiation work.
Certain radiation incidents must be reported under the Ionising Radiations Regulations or RIDDOR.
REPPIR may apply where work with radioactive substances exceeds specified levels.
Ionising-radiation controls depend on source type, activity or energy, shielding, distance, time, work classification, dose assessment, occupancy and emergency scenarios.
Ionising-radiation evidence is source-, practice-, worker- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level dose or health probability.
